Arc Length

This scene measures a curve by cutting it into straight pieces. The sum of the piece lengths is the polygonal length.

Finer partitions only make that sum grow, approaching the true length from below. The supremum over all partitions is the length of the curve. If that supremum is infinite, the curve cannot be measured.

For example, lay a 🧵 string along a winding path and measure it piece by piece, straightening each bit. The finer the pieces, the closer you get to the string's true length.

  2. The speed is constant: ∣γ′(t)∣=(−Rsin⁡t)2+(Rcos⁡t)2=R2sin⁡2t+R2cos⁡2t=Rsin⁡2t+cos⁡2t=R|\gamma'(t)| = \sqrt{(-R\sin t)^2 + (R\cos t)^2} = \sqrt{R^2\sin^2 t + R^2\cos^2 t} = R\sqrt{\sin^2 t + \cos^2 t} = R∣γ′(t)∣=(−Rsint)2+(Rcost)2​=R2sin2t+R2cos2t​=Rsin2t+cos2t​=R (for R>0R > 0R>0).

    The Pythagorean identity sin⁡2t+cos⁡2t=1\sin^2 t + \cos^2 t = 1sin2t+cos2t=1 cancels the angle dependence exactly.

    So the length of a circular arc is the radius times the subtended angle.

Show proof

  1. First insert a single point. Putting sss with ti−1<s<tit_{i-1} < s < t_iti−1​<s<ti​ into the subinterval [ti−1,ti][t_{i-1}, t_i][ti−1​,ti​] replaces that subinterval's contribution ∣γ(ti)−γ(ti−1)∣|\gamma(t_i) - \gamma(t_{i-1})|∣γ(ti​)−γ(ti−1​)∣ by ∣γ(ti)−γ(s)∣+∣γ(s)−γ(ti−1)∣|\gamma(t_i) - \gamma(s)| + |\gamma(s) - \gamma(t_{i-1})|∣γ(ti​)−γ(s)∣+∣γ(s)−γ(ti−1​)∣. Every other subinterval contributes exactly as before.

  2. Apply the triangle inequality in R2\mathbb{R}^2R2, ∣u+v∣≤∣u∣+∣v∣|u + v| \le |u| + |v|∣u+v∣≤∣u∣+∣v∣, with u=γ(ti)−γ(s)u = \gamma(t_i) - \gamma(s)u=γ(ti​)−γ(s) and v=γ(s)−γ(ti−1)v = \gamma(s) - \gamma(t_{i-1})v=γ(s)−γ(ti−1​). Then u+v=γ(ti)−γ(ti−1)u + v = \gamma(t_i) - \gamma(t_{i-1})u+v=γ(ti​)−γ(ti−1​), so ∣γ(ti)−γ(ti−1)∣≤∣γ(ti)−γ(s)∣+∣γ(s)−γ(ti−1)∣|\gamma(t_i) - \gamma(t_{i-1})| \le |\gamma(t_i) - \gamma(s)| + |\gamma(s) - \gamma(t_{i-1})|∣γ(ti​)−γ(ti−1​)∣≤∣γ(ti​)−γ(s)∣+∣γ(s)−γ(ti−1​)∣.

    Hence the new contribution is at least the old one: inserting one point never shortens the polygonal length. A single straight piece cannot beat the two bent pieces replacing it.

  3. Induction on finitely many inserted points gives the general case. If P′P'P′ refines PPP, insert the points of P′∖PP' \setminus PP′∖P one at a time to pass from PPP to P′P'P′; the length never decreases at any step, so L(P)≤L(P′)L(P) \le L(P')L(P)≤L(P′).

  4. Consequently every polygonal value lies below the supremum: L(P)≤L:=sup⁡PL(P)L(P) \le L := \sup_P L(P)L(P)≤L:=supP​L(P) for all PPP, by the very definition of a supremum.
